newsitem.title: UK: Trade cites cost as problem with unmodified soya.
newsitem.headline: Trade cites cost as problem with unmodified soya.

text.p: Traders said on Tuesday it was possible to buy soy oil guaranteed not to have been made with genetically-altered U.S. beans, but cost was a problem.

The traders were commenting on a tide of protest, mostly in Germany, against the use of soybeans that have been genetically modified by the U.S. chemicals firm of Monsanto to resist its Roundup weedkiller.
Greenpeace lobbyists in Hamburg prepared a protest against a ship due there late on Tuesday with U.S. soybeans aboard.

Up to two percent of the U.S. crop consists of modified beans but these are often mixed in with others. German activists want processors to insist on separating them out and say food products made from modified soya should be clearly labelled.

"It is possible to separate new soybeans from traditional ones and U.S. sources tell us there are now beans available which are guaranteed to be free of genetic manipulation," said Joerg Nauman of Greenpeace.

A vegetable oil trader said oil was being offered with three independent certificates guaranteeing it was not made from modified soybeans. These came from the transport company which moved beans from the farm, the grain elevator and a laboratory.
One such laboratory was Iowa-based Genetic ID, founded a little over two months ago and now working at capacity with orders from brokers on both sides of the Atlantic.
It says the genetic code of all unaltered soybean is identical. If foreign DNA has been spliced in to the natural sequence, it could be detected by Genetic ID technology.

"The tests, plus separate transport and storage add about $15 a tonne to the cost of soybeans shipped into Europe but the sellers can't get any more for their oil and meal than the market will allow," one said.
Current prices are around $276 per tonne.
Elsewhere in Europe on Tuesday the Dutch Food and Drink Industry Association said in a statement that members would use genetically-altered soya.
"This month, soybeans will be imported into the Netherlands which have been produced with the help of modern bio-technology.
"The Dutch food sector only processes and sells products that are safe for the consumer and which have government approval," the Nederlandse Voedingsmiddelen Industrie said.
It said health authorities in the United States, UK, European Union, Canada and Japan had also approved the product.
German Social Democrat MP Liesel Hartenstein issued a statement saying that consumers "must not be degraded into guinea pigs".
She demanded segregation of soybeans, strict labelling and research assessing health risks from transgenic food.
